subject: Chemistry
title: Uranium: From Paint to Power
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Uranium: From Paint to Power.

hook.text: Before it powered reactors, uranium was used to make bright orange glaze for dinner plates.

buildup.text: Martin Klaproth discovered uranium in 1789 and named it after the planet Uranus, discovered eight years earlier.

discovery.text: Henri Becquerel found in 1896 that uranium emits invisible rays—the discovery of radioactivity.

twist.text: For decades, uranium was a curiosity. Then Hahn and Strassmann split its nucleus in 1938—nuclear fission.

climax.text: Uranium now fuels power plants generating 10% of the world's electricity. Same element, new purpose.

punchline.text: Orange plates to nuclear power. Uranium found its real purpose.

quiz.question: What was uranium used for before nuclear energy?
options: As a colorant for ceramic glazes and glass

details.summary: Uranium was discovered by Martin Klaproth in 1789 and existed as a minor curiosity used mainly in yellow glass and ceramic glazes for over a century..
details.whyItMatters: Uranium's transformation from decorative material to world-changing power source illustrates how scientific discovery can instantly revolutionize an element's significance. Nuclear energy from uranium generates about 10% of global electricity.
takeaways: Uranium was used in yellow glass and ceramic glazes for over a hundred years
Nuclear fission's discovery in 1938 made uranium strategically critical overnight
Uranium-235 powers both nuclear weapons and civilian nuclear reactors

faq.question: How does uranium produce energy through nuclear fission?
faq.answer: When a neutron strikes uranium-235, the nucleus splits into two lighter elements, releasing energy and additional neutrons. These neutrons trigger more fissions in a chain reaction..

faq.question: Why was uranium used in glassware and ceramics before nuclear energy?
faq.answer: Uranium oxide produces a distinctive fluorescent yellow-green color in glass that cannot be replicated with other colorants. Uranium-glazed ceramics, called Fiestaware, were popular in the early 20th century..
